extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors of the Philosophical Transactions: natural philosophers, physicians, and mathematicians (late 17th century learned audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Abridged summaries of multiple short communications in natural philosophy (medical case reports, physiognomy discourse, natural history, and mathematical methods) from a Philosophical Transactions volume, intended to record observations, methods, and results for fellow scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious inference on epidemic direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whence we may reasonably infer, that these spreading epidemic distempers take their progress from east to west. But this should be further confirmed by more frequent observations, before we may safely determine any thing on this head generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize direction of epidemic spread from only a couple instances; require more frequent observations across locations and times to confirm a general rule. The author notes consistency in two instances but explicitly cautions further confirmation is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptomology of the 1688 transient fever
rubrics_metrics.description: It began ... with a chillness and shivering all over, like that of an ague, but not so violent, which soon broke out into a dry burning heat, with great uneasiness, that commonly confined the patients to their beds ... they complained likewise of giddiness, and a dull pain in the head, chiefly about the eyes, with wandering pains in their limbs, and about the small of the back, a soreness all over their flesh, a loss of appetite, a nausea, and an unusual ill taste in the mouth, yet little or no thirst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this constellation of signs (initial chill/shiver, transition to dry burning heat, headache/giddiness, limb/back pains, general soreness, appetite loss, nausea, altered taste, little thirst) to recognize this transient epidemic fever; many symptoms are transient and resolve within days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment guidance for the 1688 transient fever
rubrics_metrics.description: About the 2d day of the distemper, the patient usually of himself fell into a sweat, unless it was prevented by letting blood, which, however beneficial in other fevers, manifestly retarded the progress of this; and if the sweat was encouraged for 5 or 6 hours, by laying on more clothes, or taking some sudorific medicine, most of the complaints would entirely disappear, or at least very much abate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage sweating (hot coverings or sudorifics) rather than bloodletting in this fever: bloodletting tended to prevent the natural sweat and retarded recovery. Clinical management emphasizes promoting perspiration early (circa day 2) to shorten course or abate symptoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prognosis and course of the 1688 fever
rubrics_metrics.description: The giddiness of the head and want of appetite would often continue some days after, but with the use of the open fresh air, they certainly in 4 or 5 days at farthest recovered, and were perfectly well ... of 1000 that were seized with it, I believe scarcely one died; and by the middle of August following it wholly disappeared; so that its whole period was about 7 weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect mostly mild, self-limited course: most patients recover in 4–5 days (residual symptoms possible), extremely low mortality reported (~<1/1000), and outbreak duration on population level ~7 weeks. Fresh air recommended for convalescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autopsy procedure and detection of gall-bladder stone
rubrics_metrics.description: After throwing up the sternum, and inspecting the parts contained in the cavity of the breast... Beneath the diaphragm, in the cavity of the abdomen, I found ... the vesica bilaria seemed full of bile; but, more curiously examining it by the touch, I found by the interposition of a solid body ... I opened the vesica, and with my forceps extracted a stone very beautifully crusted over with crystallized salts of various figures ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic dissection: inspect thoracic organs, then abdominal cavity beneath diaphragm; palpation of gallbladder for induration/stone; confirm by opening vesica biliaris and extract with forceps; document stone characteristics (size, weight, crystallized salt crusting) and associated organ findings (enlarged spleen, abscesses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Craig's quadrature method (quadratrix approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author gives a general method for determining the quadratures of curvilinear spaces, which he shows may always be done, by finding another curve-line, from the known property of its tangent; which curve-line he therefore calls the quadratrix of the proposed space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the quadratrix— a constructed curve derived from tangent properties— to reduce quadrature problems. The treatise also proposes a new method of finding infinite series by assuming an arbitrary series with unknown coefficients and determining them in progress; includes worked examples and links to contemporary methods (Leibnitz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical/geometrical check for quadrature deficiency or excess
rubrics_metrics.description: He concludes this first part with a discourse concerning the analytical expression of quadratures, wherein is shown, that though the area answering to the abscissa be that which is commonly sought, yet the general quadrature found by his method is for the most part either greater or less: therefore he gives both a geometrical and analytical rule for knowing whether the said general quadrature be deficient or exceeding, and what that deficient or exceeding quantity is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using the quadratrix/general method, apply the provided geometrical and analytical tests to determine whether a found quadrature over- or under-estimates the desired area, and to compute the magnitude of the discrepancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for determining geometric loci by equation comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerning the geometric loci: showing how to determine any solid locus, by comparing the equation with a general theorem comprehending all loci of that kind: thus avoiding all those rules about the reduction of the given equation, and the variety of the signs + and - , which have hitherto rendered this part of geometry so troublesome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer comparing a problem's equation with a broad general theorem for that class of loci rather than performing repeated algebraic reductions and sign manipulations; this structural comparison simplifies locus determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy principle: facial impressions via animal spirits and habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft wax cannot receive more numerous and various impressions, than are imprinted on the human face by objects moving the affections ... the animal spirits, moved in the sensory by an object, continue their motion to the brain; whence the motion is propagated to this or that particular part of the body ... by repeated acts or by frequent entertaining the ideas of a favourite passion or vice ... the face is so often put into that posture which attends such acts, that the animal spirits find such passages into its nerves, that it is sometimes unalterably set ... but most commonly such habit is contracted, that the face falls insensibly into that posture ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use changes or habitual postures of the face as indicators of underlying passions, habits, or frequent mental states, recognizing that ideas/images can have similar effects as real objects (e.g., dreams). However, the author cautions against absolute inference—exceptions exist (virtuous persons under unpromising outsides).

rubrics_metrics.name: General method for finding roots by assuming z = a ± e
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the root z of any equation be supposed to be composed of two terms a + or - e, of which a is assumed as near as may be to z ... then let the quantity a + or - e be raised to all the powers of z found in the given equation, and affixing to each the corresponding numeral co-efficients. Then ... the homogeneum comparationis, and let the difference be + b. Next, take the sum of all the co-efficients of e in the second column, which put = s. Lastly, collect together all the co-efficients of e^2 ... the sum of which call t. Then will the near value of the root z be thus, viz. in the rational form, z = a - (b/s) ... and z = a + (some irrational form involving s and t) ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: choose a near integer a, expand (a ± e)^n to match equation terms, collect the homogeneum comparationis to get b, sum coefficients of e (s) and e^2 (t); compute rational approximation z ≈ a - b/s or the more accurate irrational form using s and t; ignore higher powers of e initially because e is small. Iterate with updated a as needed. The method yields rapid convergence (triples figures per repetition in some forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of powers and sign rules for a ± e expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: A convenient help ... a general table, exhibiting all the powers of a ± e ... But if it should be a - e = z, the table would still be composed of the same terms, but only the odd powers of e must be negative, as e, e^3, e^5, &c. and the even powers, e^2, e^4, e^6, &c. must still be positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided table of expansions for powers of (a ± e) as a reference when forming the homogeneum and coefficient sums; remember sign alternation when using (a - e) versus (a + e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations for pure powers (cubic, 5th, etc.): rational vs irrational forms
rubrics_metrics.description: When extracting roots of pure powers: the irrational form gives a formula that comes rather nearer the truth than the rational, but errs in point of excess, as the other in defect ... the irrational form seems more commodious for practice, since the repetition of the calculus is only the continual addition or subtraction of the small supplement e as it becomes known; so that by either form the figures already known, in extracting the root, are at least tripled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cubic and higher pure powers use both rational and irrational approximations: expect the irrational form to slightly overestimate (excess) and the rational to underestimate (defect). The irrational form is often preferred in practice because it allows fast iterative refinement, quickly multiplying the number of known correct digits per step.

rubrics_metrics.name: General proportional formula for near n-th root
rubrics_metrics.description: Or, in a proportion it is, as (n + 1) times the nearest power, added to (n — 1) times the given number : (n + 1) N + (n — 1) a^ = r the root sought ; that is, in words, as n + 1 times the nearest power, added to n — 1 times the given number, is to n + 1 times the given number added to n — 1 times the nearest power, so is the near assumed root to the root required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this general proportion to compute a near approximation of an n-th root: combine weighted averages of the nearest complete power and the given number to produce an initial near root, then refine using the a ± e expansion method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining sign of correction term and iteration advice
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign of e is determined by the sign of the quantity b : for the resolvend being taken away from the homogeneum formed of a, the sign of s e, and therefore of the parts prevailing in its composition, will always be contrary to the sign of the difference b : hence it will appear whether it should be - e or + e, or whether a be assumed greater or less than the true root. ... the calculation may be continued as far as we please, keeping still the same coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sign of b to decide whether a was assumed too large (e negative) or too small (e positive), adjust signs of odd-power terms accordingly, and iterate: substitute improved z as new hypothesis to obtain arbitrarily accurate roots while retaining previously computed coefficients for efficiency. Small corrective fractions may be added/subtracted for fine tuning.
